questions.q: What structurally distinguishes 'quantum as a coprocessor' (Pattern A) from 'quantum as the whole program' (Pattern B)?
options: Pattern A calls the QPU for a bounded sub-task inside a classical-controlled loop/application; Pattern B expresses the entire algorithm as one circuit with no iterative classical feedback
Pattern A never uses a QPU at all; Pattern B uses only QPUs
Pattern A is slower than Pattern B in every case
There is no real difference; both terms describe the same architecture
questions.explain: Pattern A treats the QPU like a GPU-style accelerator invoked for specific calls within classical control flow (e.g., the variational loop). Pattern B is a single circuit (or short fixed sequence) that IS the algorithm end to end, with no classical optimizer driving iteration.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say Pattern B (quantum as the whole program) is rare in production today?
options: Problems where it applies at useful scale (e.g., Shor's-algorithm-scale factoring) require far more qubits and lower error rates than current hardware provides
Because no classical code is allowed in Pattern B architectures
Because cloud providers do not permit single-circuit submissions
Because Pattern B is actually the more common production pattern, not Pattern A
questions.explain: Pattern B's classic use cases (true Grover-speedup search, Shor's-scale factoring) need hardware scale and fault tolerance that doesn't exist yet, so it remains mostly a research-stage pattern rather than something shipped in production.

questions.q: In the lesson's 20-truck routing example, why is the Pattern A (QAOA + classical optimizer) approach buildable today while the Pattern B approach is not?
options: Pattern A only requires a QPU capable of evaluating a QUBO cost function within an iterative loop, while Pattern B would require fault-tolerant qubits at a scale that doesn't exist for a problem of this size
Pattern A requires no quantum hardware at all
Pattern B is actually easier to build but more expensive
Both approaches are equally buildable; the lesson treats them as interchangeable
questions.explain: Pattern A bounds the QPU's role to repeated cost-function evaluations inside a classical loop -- achievable on current hardware. Pattern B would need a single circuit to directly yield the optimal route, which requires a scale of fault-tolerant hardware not available today.

questions.q: According to the comparison table, where does most of the engineering effort go in a Pattern A (coprocessor) project versus a Pattern B (whole-program) project?
options: Pattern A: classical orchestration, optimizer tuning, and cost/latency management. Pattern B: circuit design and correctness
Pattern A: circuit design only. Pattern B: classical orchestration only
Both patterns require identical effort distribution
Pattern A requires no engineering effort since the QPU does all the work
questions.explain: Because Pattern A's correctness and performance hinge on the classical loop (as shown in the variational loop lesson), most effort goes there. Pattern B's correctness hinges almost entirely on the circuit itself, since there's no classical feedback loop to debug.

questions.q: A manager wants to scope factoring 2048-bit RSA keys with Shor's algorithm as a near-term, no-classical-loop production project. What is the correct response based on this lesson?
options: Explain that this is a Pattern B use case requiring a scale of fault-tolerant qubits far beyond current hardware, so it isn't a near-term buildable project regardless of engineering skill
Agree and start scoping -- Pattern B projects are simpler because there's no classical loop to build
Tell them it's buildable today as long as the team hires more quantum optimizer specialists
Tell them to switch to a QAOA-based coprocessor pattern, since that is functionally identical to Shor's algorithm
questions.explain: The hardware, not the architecture choice, is the blocker: full-scale Shor's algorithm for 2048-bit RSA is a Pattern B problem that needs far more fault-tolerant qubits than exist today. The right answer sets expectations about hardware readiness, not team skill.
